title: Cardiovascular Comprehensive Set 1: Special Circulation (Short answer)

questions.prompt: Define autoregulation and identify three organs that prominently exhibit this phenomenon.
questions.modelAnswer: Autoregulation is the maintenance of constant blood flow despite changes in perfusion pressure; it is prominent in the heart, brain, and kidney.

questions.prompt: Explain the myogenic hypothesis of autoregulation in terms of the relationship between transmural pressure and vascular smooth muscle.
questions.modelAnswer: It states that vascular smooth muscle contracts when stretched; an increase in pressure stretches the arteriole, causing it to constrict and increase resistance to maintain constant flow.

questions.prompt: How does the metabolic hypothesis explain the matching of blood flow to the oxygen demand of a tissue?
questions.modelAnswer: Metabolic activity produces vasodilator metabolites; as demand for O2 increases, these metabolites accumulate and dilate arterioles to increase O2 delivery.

questions.prompt: List four specific vasodilator metabolites produced during periods of high metabolic activity.
questions.modelAnswer: CO2, H^+, K^+, lactate, and adenosine.

questions.prompt: What is active hyperemia, and how does it differ from reactive hyperemia?
questions.modelAnswer: Active hyperemia occurs when flow is proportional to metabolic activity; reactive hyperemia is an increase in flow following a period of occlusion.

questions.prompt: Identify the most important local metabolic factors responsible for regulating coronary blood flow.
questions.modelAnswer: Adenosine and hypoxia (low P_(O2)).

questions.prompt: During which phase of the cardiac cycle is left ventricular coronary blood flow lowest, and what is the mechanical cause?
questions.modelAnswer: Systole, because the contracting myocardium mechanically compresses the coronary blood vessels.

questions.prompt: Which metabolic byproduct is the most important local vasodilator for the cerebral circulation?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide (CO2).

questions.prompt: Explain why many circulating vasoactive substances in the systemic blood have little or no effect on cerebral blood flow.
questions.modelAnswer: The blood-brain barrier is impermeable to many large or polar vasoactive substances.

questions.prompt: Describe the Cushing reaction in terms of the stimulus and the resulting effect on systemic arterial pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebral ischemia (increased intracranial pressure) stimulates the vasomotor center to produce an intense increase in mean arterial pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the primary regulator of skeletal muscle blood flow at rest?
questions.modelAnswer: The sympathetic nervous system (vasoconstrictor tone).

questions.prompt: Which specific autonomic receptors on skeletal muscle arterioles mediate vasoconstriction, and which mediate vasodilation?
questions.modelAnswer: α1receptors mediate vasoconstriction; β2  receptors (activated by epinephrine) mediate vasodilation.

questions.prompt: Identify the three local metabolites primarily responsible for vasodilation in exercising skeletal muscle.
questions.modelAnswer: Lactate, adenosine, and K^+.

questions.prompt: What is the principal physiological function of the sympathetic innervation of skin blood vessels?
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature regulation.

questions.prompt: How does the anterior hypothalamus coordinate heat dissipation through the cutaneous circulation when body temperature increases?
questions.modelAnswer: It decreases sympathetic tone to skin vessels (causing vasodilation) and increases sympathetic cholinergic activity to sweat glands.

questions.prompt: Describe the components of the "triple response" in the skin following trauma and identify the chemical responsible for the "wheal".
questions.modelAnswer: A red line, a red flare, and a wheal; the wheal is caused by histamine.

questions.prompt: Contrast the effect of hypoxia on the pulmonary vasculature with its effect on most other systemic vascular beds.
questions.modelAnswer: Hypoxia causes vasoconstriction in the pulmonary circulation but vasodilation in most systemic circulations.

questions.prompt: By what cellular mechanism does nitric oxide (NO) produce relaxation of vascular smooth muscle?
questions.modelAnswer: It activates guanylate cyclase, increasing cGMP, which causes relaxation.

questions.prompt: How do histamine and bradykinin alter Starling forces to produce local edema?
questions.modelAnswer: They cause arteriolar dilation and venous constriction, which increases capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc ), favoring filtration.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of low-dose dopamine on renal, splanchnic, and cerebral arterioles?
questions.modelAnswer: It dilates these arterioles, protecting blood flow to critical organs.

questions.prompt: Explain the "vasomotor tone" (basal tone) in the context of arteriolar smooth muscle.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the state of tonic (continuous) contraction of arteriolar smooth muscle maintained by sympathetic adrenergic nerves.

questions.prompt: How does an increase in intracranial pressure lead to a decrease in brain oxygenation?
questions.modelAnswer: It compresses cerebral veins, raising capillary pressure and causing cerebral edema, which further increases pressure and ischemia.

questions.prompt: In the context of parallel resistance, what is the effect of adding a new blood vessel to an organ's circulation on the total resistance of that organ?
questions.modelAnswer: Total resistance decreases.

questions.prompt: Identify the role of serotonin in the response to blood vessel damage.
questions.modelAnswer: It causes local vasoconstriction to reduce blood loss after vessel damage.

questions.prompt: Explain why the filtration fraction increases when the efferent arteriole is constricted.
questions.modelAnswer: It increases PGC  (glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure), which increases GFR, while simultaneously decreasing RPF.
